title: Imagining the Unlikely: Si + Imperfect Subjunctive

sections.title: Open or imagined?
sections.content: You know *si* with the present from B1 Unit 8: *Si llueve, nos quedamos en casa* treats the rain as a real possibility. You also know from B1 Unit 4 that *si* + the imperfect subjunctive + the conditional pictures something unlikely, imaginary or contrary to the facts: *Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría más*. At B2 the skill is choosing between the two on purpose. With the present, the condition is open: it may well happen. With the imperfect subjunctive you keep it at a distance: you think it is unlikely, or you are only playing with the idea. The imperfect subjunctive here does not refer to the past: *Si ganara mañana…* is about tomorrow.

sections.title: Open or imagined
rows: Si llueve mañana, nos quedaremos en casa.
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home. (open)
Si lloviera mañana, nos quedaríamos en casa.
If it were to rain tomorrow, we would stay at home. (unlikely, or just imagined)
If I have time, I will call you. (it may well happen)
If I had time, I would call you. (I probably do not)

sections.title: The pattern
rows: -ra or -se form in the si clause
Si tuviera tiempo = Si tuviese tiempo.
the si clause can come second
Viviríamos en el campo si pudiéramos elegir.

items.spanish: Si el gobierno ofreciera ayuda, muchas familias podrían comprar su casa.
items.english: If the government offered help, many families could buy their home.

items.spanish: Si mañana nevara en la ciudad, cerrarían las escuelas.
items.english: If it snowed in the city tomorrow, they would close the schools.

items.spanish: Viviríamos en el campo si pudiéramos elegir.
items.english: We would live in the countryside if we could choose.

sections.content: Put the conditional only in the main clause, never after *si*: *Si tendría dinero* is wrong, so say *Si tuviera dinero*. The *-ra* and *-se* forms are interchangeable here, but *-ra* is the one you will hear most. This unit stays with the present and the future.
